titulo.texto: Traditional Nahua huipil from the Huasteca of Hidalgo

frase_gancho.texto: A white huipil where birds, corn, and four-pointed stars bloom.

puente_narrativo.texto: From cloth we move on to paper. Look for a brown sheet covered with tiny scenes of festivals, weddings, and work in the fields, drawn in black ink.

guion_corto.texto: This huipil belongs to the Nahua women of the Huasteca, in the state of Hidalgo. It is a straight-cut garment of white cotton, with a square neckline. It is covered with cross-stitch embroidery in very bright threads: carmine red, Mexican pink, orange, green, and turquoise blue. Look closely at the designs: wildflowers, birds, climbing vines, corn plants, and four-pointed stars. For Nahua women, embroidering is a way of drawing the world around them: the cornfield, the hills, and the animals that live there. This garment is worn at weddings, at baptisms, and at Xantolo, the festival of the dead.

guion_largo.texto:
If you have made it this far, you have walked through almost the whole museum, and now it is time to greet the descendants of the Mexica. The Nahua are the largest Indigenous people in the country: it is estimated that more than a million and a half people speak Nahuatl. They do not live in just one place: there are Nahua communities in the Huasteca, in the northern highlands of Puebla, in Guerrero, in Morelos, in the State of Mexico, in Veracruz, and even on the outskirts of Mexico City.

Without realizing it, you already speak a little of their language. Chapulín, guajolote, tianguis, petate, mecate, and papalote come from Nahuatl, and papalote means “butterfly.” In the first hall upstairs you saw that chocolate, tomato, and avocado come from there too. Every time you ask for a guajolote at the market, you are using a word that was already spoken in the market of Tlatelolco.

Many Nahua call themselves macehuales. In Mexica times the word designated common people, as opposed to the nobility, and it has been explained as “the deserved ones”: those who exist because the gods did penance for them. It is the story of the Fifth Sun, which you saw at the [Sun Stone](mna_s06_piedra_sol). When a Nahua woman introduces herself as a macehual, she quietly recalls that story of sacrifice and gratitude.

Look at the huipil calmly. Its shape is simple, but the embroidery transforms it. Cross-stitch makes it possible to draw with great precision, because each cross is like a small dot of color in an image, similar to the pixels on a screen. With thousands of crosses, flowers, birds, and plants take shape. Girls learn by watching their mothers and grandmothers, and over the years they develop their own designs.

The designs have a language. Among the flowers, you may find the cempasúchil, the same one from the [Xantolo arch](mna_s18_altar_xantolo). There are corn plants, which are the foundation of life. And there are four-pointed stars, which can be related to the four directions, the same idea you saw in the four-petaled flower of the [Teenek quechquémitl](mna_s18_dhubem_huasteco) and in the four posts of the Maya house. A garment of white cloth thus holds a way of ordering the universe.

This is the same Huasteca region where you saw the Teenek quechquémitl. The Nahua and the Teenek are neighbors: they share cross-stitch, intense colors, and festivals such as Xantolo. What changes is the garment: here, a huipil, and there, a quechquémitl. Their languages also differ, coming from distinct families, one from the Nahuatl family and the other from the Maya family. Two peoples, two languages, one shared landscape.

These garments are made at home, over many months, between daily chores. They are first worn at important festivals, and sometimes they are inherited. When a woman puts on her embroidered huipil for a wedding or a baptism, she is not just getting dressed: she is wearing her own history and that of her family.

It is the last of the garments on this journey, and it sums up everything you have seen: thread, memory, and pride. From the backstrap loom in the first hall upstairs to the Nahua huipil here, there is one and the same gesture: turning a piece of cloth into a way of saying who you are.

texto: Look for the four-pointed stars among the flowers
Find an embroidered corn plant and a bird
Count how many different colors the embroidery has

texto.Region: Huasteca of Hidalgo (Huejutla de Reyes, Atlapexco)
texto.Technique/Material: Cotton muslin embroidered by hand in cross-stitch with multicolored thread
texto.Function: Everyday formal attire, agricultural celebrations, and the Xantolo festival

texto.pregunta: Myth: The Nahua are a people of the past, who disappeared with the Mexica.
texto.respuesta: Reality: Today they are the largest Indigenous people in Mexico: more than a million and a half people speak Nahuatl.
